content:
Hi, I'm a hobbyist Lean user who's new to this community, and I'd appreciate feedback on what, if there's interest, may be my first contribution: a completion of Lean's omega tactic for quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic.

The current implementation's documentation indicates that it performs real Fourier-Motzkin elimination but does not implement Pugh's dark and grey shadows. As such, it can fail on unsatisfiable integer problems whose rational shadow remains satisfiable. The following example (Pugh's nightmare) fails under omega and succeeds under grind:

example (x y : Int)
    (h₁ : 27 ≤ 11 * x + 13 * y)
    (h₂ : 11 * x + 13 * y ≤ 45)
    (h₃ : -10 ≤ 7 * x - 9 * y)
    (h₄ : 7 * x - 9 * y ≤ 4) : False := by
  omega

I have a working prototype (https://github.com/klittlepage/lean4/tree/omega-with-shadows) that implements a complete Pugh-style dark/grey-shadow decision procedure, together with constructive satisfying models, proof-free checked refutations, proved well-founded termination, and an exact proof-producing adapter to Lean's existing omega frontend.

Given that grind already works on QF_LIA problems, completing omega isn't necessarily a game changer. But one possible downstream use is verifiable SMT(LIA) workflows and MILP presolve/reformulation, which is what got me interested in adding this tactic. It allows an external SMT solver to remain an untrusted search engine and have Lean check the result against the original reflected formula:

  • A sat result can be checked by evaluating the supplied integer model;
  • Small or residual unsat obligations can be decided again by the verified core;
  • Future compact arithmetic traces could be checked against the same normalization and semantics, without trusting the external solver's implementation.

The POC

  • Supports linear integer expressions, inequalities, equality, divisibility, and boolean combinations;
  • Returns either a concrete satisfying valuation or a proof-free checked refutation;
  • Proves soundness and completeness for its direct surface grammar;
  • Uses well-founded recursion rather than arbitrary fuel;
  • Implements exact quotient introduction, terminating equality reduction, and complete finite dark/grey-shadow search with model reconstruction.

An adapter translates the residual Omega.Problem produced by the existing frontend into the verified conjunction solver. Existing successful proofs follow the current path, while a residual problem that the real-shadow engine cannot close is sent to the verified backend before omega reports failure. The prototype also has a qflia entry point that selects the verified backend first, although whether this deserves a new public tactic name is one of the questions for this discussion.

The tactic-level completeness claim remains conditional on the existing frontend. The direct core is complete for its declared QF_LIA grammar, but the tactic does not thereby become complete for expressions that preprocessing does not translate into integer-linear constraints.

Questions I'd especially value feedback on

This is my first time popping the hood on the lean4 core, so apologies if the answers to some of these are obvious.

  1. Is a separate total Std.Tactic.QFLIA core preferable to adding dark and grey shadows directly to the existing MetaM implementation?
  2. Should the total model/checker API be public in Std, internal to the tactic implementation, or developed outside the Lean repository first?
  3. Is a public qflia tactic useful for exposing the verified-first behavior, or should this begin as an option or internal test entry point?
  4. Is preserving the current legacy-first omega path the right compatibility strategy, or would maintainers prefer eventual replacement by the verified backend?
  5. Which performance and proof-size comparisons would be most useful for evaluating the design?
  6. Would a reusable checked LIA feasibility core be useful to existing SMT, verification, or optimization projects, and what certificate interface would those projects need?

The medium-term goal is to make omega a core-internal tactic that is only used in core files which are so early that grind is not available yet, and completely unavailable outside of core. For this reason, core is not interested in any changes to the omega tactic.

From what you're written I don't see any reason why your development should be part of core, instead of your own library.

@Julia Markus Himmel I'm not following. The POC is in direct response to TODOs in the omega source, and does not use grind. It has no dependencies, it simply completes the currently incomplete omega algorithm documented as TODO/future work.
What I'm saying is that omega as a public tactic will be retired and the implementation should be considered frozen. The TODOs in the code are old and we are not interested in seeing them resolved.
Ah, got it, that makes sense. Thanks, I'll keep it as a library in that case, unless you're aware of something else in this space? I couldn't find anything.
